Gastrocnemius Contracture
 CORE
September 25, 2025
John G. Anderson, MD, FAAOS (2020–present)
Jacob Markel, MD (2025–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Understand the relevant anatomy of the gastrocnemius tendon with respect to its innervation
and blood supply, origin and insertion, and musculotendinous unit.
Understand how to perform and the implications of the Silfverskiöld test.
Identify indications for possible gastrocnemius recession.
Understand possible complications of surgical management and gastrocnemius recession.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
The prevalence and importance of gastrocnemius contractures is highly controversial and has
been disputed.




NOTES

Multiple pathologic foot and ankle conditions are believed to be caused by forefoot, midfoot,
and hindfoot mechanical overload. Pathology is believed to occur secondary to
gastrocnemius muscle contracture, which results in a muscular imbalance that alters gait
mechanics, increases recruitment of the toe extensor musculature, and increases forefoot
pathologic pressure.
Another common diagnosis for the condition, equinus contracture, describes the vertical
orientation of the tibiotalar joint, which is similar to that observed in horse anatomy. This
orientation, although advantageous for quadrupedal motion, is problematic for human
bipedal motion. During bipedal motion, passive dorsiflexion with an extended knee is
important, especially during the second (rocker) phase of gait.
With a tight gastrocnemius muscle, the heel elevates from the ground, prematurely
transferring more weight for a prolonged period to the midfoot, the plantar fascia, and
ultimately the forefoot.
The consequence of this overload is tension of the soft tissue of the posterior calf and the
plantar aspect of the foot, contributing to insertional and non-insertional Achilles
tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis, neuromas, metatarsalgia, and progressive arch collapse.
Epidemiology
Patel and DiGiovanni1 identified an 88% incidence of gastrocnemius contractures
(characterized by <10° of dorsiflexion on the Silfverskiöld test) in patients with symptomatic
foot pain compared with only 44% in asymptomatic controls.
Anatomy
Superficial Posterior Compartment (Tibial Nerve)
The gastrocnemius muscle and tendon reside in the superficial posterior compartment of the
leg along with the soleus and plantaris muscles and is innervated by the tibial nerve.

Superficial Compartment (Tibial Nerve)
The muscle is a component of what is known as the triceps surae. The gastrocnemius
contributes two muscle bellies and one tendon to the triceps surae complex, whereas
the soleus contributes one muscle belly and one tendon to the triceps surae complex.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
2/19

The muscle belly of the soleus continues much more distal along the tibia than the
gastrocnemius muscle fibers. Before the gastrocnemius and soleus tendons merge, they
glide independently. The two tendons merge at the distal two-thirds of the calf (typically
6 to 9 cm proximal to the point of calcaneal insertion) to become the Achilles tendon.
The calcaneal insertion of the Achilles tendon is 1.2 to 2.5 cm wide and approximately 5
to 6 mm thick, depending on the individual’s size.2,3 The fibers of the Achilles tendon
rotate 90° to insert into the posterior aspect of the calcaneus. The medial and lateral
heads of the gastrocnemius muscle (origin at medial and femoral condyles, respectively)
are the only components that cross the knee joint; therefore, they can be isolated via the
Silfverskiöld test.
Vasculature: Lateral and Medial Sural Arteries (Popliteal Artery)
The medial and lateral heads of the gastrocnemius are supplied by the lateral and medial sural
arteries, which are direct branches of the popliteal artery.2,3
Function
Heel inverter
The gastrocnemius tendon runs just medial to the hindfoot axis of rotation and, therefore,
acts as an inverter of the heel (with synergistic effects of the soleus muscle).
Plantar flexion
The gastrocnemius is a major plantar flexor of the ankle joint with the knee extended.
Knee flexion
It also acts as a weak knee flexor given that musculotendinous unit crosses the knee and
inserts on the posterior femoral condyles.
Sural Nerve
The sural nerve initially runs midline in the calf over the gastrocnemius-soleus muscle until
approximately the musculotendinous junction, the location at which it crosses to the lateral
side of the tendon (Figure 1).

Figure 1 Illustration of the leg shows the gastrocnemius-soleus complex. A = lateral head of the
gastrocnemius muscle, B = sural nerve, C = medial head of the gastrocnemius muscle, D =
gastrocnemius tendon (aponeurosis), E = soleus, F = Achilles tendon. (Reproduced from
Abdulmassih S, Phisitkul P, Femino JE, Amendola A: Triceps surae contracture: Implications for
foot and ankle surgery. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2013;21[7]:398-407).

Sural Nerve
The sural nerve is at risk during approaches and surgical recession of the gastrocnemius
tendon. The sural nerve is located along the lateral aspect of the triceps surae complex
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
4/19

and is at risk during surgical approaches and recession of the gastrocnemius tendon
because it lies close to the gastrocnemius fascia. The sural nerve is a terminal branch of
the peroneal nerve and provides sensation to the lateral aspect of the leg and foot. In an
anatomic study by Pinney et al,4 the sural nerve was superficial to the fascia in 42.5% of
the extremities and deep to the fascia in 57.5% of the extremities. Any injury to the sural
nerve may result in numbness and a painful neuroma. The sural nerve must be
identified and protected during gastrocnemius release.
Classification
Although Patel and DiGiovanni1 identified an 88% incidence of gastrocnemius contractures
(characterized by <10° of dorsiflexion on the Silfverskiöld test) in patients with symptomatic
foot pain compared with only 44% in asymptomatic controls, no universally accepted degree of
limited dorsiflexion defines gastrocnemius contracture.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Symptoms may include pain, swelling, and warmth in patients with insertional or non-
insertional Achilles tendinopathy or plantar fasciitis.
Patients may report a history of toe walking, especially pediatric patients, or difficulty placing
the heel on the ground.
Physical Examination
Pathologic (positive) Silfverskiöld test
An isolated gastrocnemius contracture is measured and differentiated from a
gastrocnemius/soleus contracture via the Silfverskiöld test.
The Silfverskiöld test evaluates the anatomic etiology of equinus contracture of the ankle.
This assessment is performed by measuring dorsiflexion of the foot with the knee flexed and
then extended (Figure 2).

9/3/26, 4:16 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012

Figure 2 Clinical photographs show the Silfverskiöld test. A, Incorrect method of positioning the
foot for physical examination. B, Correct technique, with the foot held inverted to lock the
transverse tarsal joint. C, Dorsiflexion with the knee in extension. D, Dorsiflexion with the knee in
flexion. (Reproduced from Bohay DR, Anderson JG, Cheney NA, Rust CL: Metatarsal osteotomy to
manage metatarsal prominence, in Alexander IJ, Bluman EM, Greisberg JK, eds: Advanced
Reconstruction: Foot and Ankle, ed 2. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons,
2015, pp 47-54.)

Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
6/19

A gastrocnemius contracture is identified if dorsiflexion is less than 10° with the knee
extended that improves with the knee flexed. During the terminal phase of stance, 10° of
passive dorsiflexion with the knee extended is required for tibial advancement.
Neurovascular Examination
Semmes-Weinstein 5.07 (10 g) monofilament testing is important to evaluate for possible
neuropathy.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiography
Appropriate standard radiographic images (AP and lateral view of the foot and AP, mortise,
and lateral views of the ankle) dictated by the anatomic location of the pain often are
obtained to evaluate for concomitant foot and ankle pathology.
Advanced imaging studies (CT, MRI, or bone scanning)
Rarely indicated for the work up of gastrocnemius contracture
Pathology
Idiopathic or secondary to trauma
Isolated gastrocnemius contracture may be idiopathic or secondary to trauma or syndromic
(eg, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease). The clinical ramifications of the prevalence and
importance of gastrocnemius contractures is controversial and has been disputed. Multiple
pathologic foot and ankle conditions are believed to be caused by forefoot, midfoot, and
hindfoot mechanical overload thought to occur secondary to gastrocnemius muscle
contracture, which results in a muscular imbalance that alters gait mechanics, increases
recruitment of the toe extensor musculature, and increases forefoot pathologic pressure
(Figure 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
7/19

Figure 3 Drawings of the leg show load patterns during gait. The anticipated variation in forefoot
and midfoot loading during late-stance–phase gait between patients with a normal
gastrocnemius (ie, normal gastrocnemius length; left) and patients with an abnormal
gastrocnemius (ie, contracted gastrocnemius; right) is highlighted. (Reproduced with permission
from DiGiovanni CW, Kuo R, Tejwani N, et al: Isolated gastrocnemius tightness. J Bone Joint Surg
Am 2002;84[6]:962-970.)
Forefoot overload and progressive arch collapse
The consequence of this overload is tension of the soft tissue of the posterior calf and the
plantar aspect of the foot, contributing to insertional and non-insertional Achilles
tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis, neuromas, metatarsalgia, and progressive arch collapse. This
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
8/19

pathologic gastrocnemius contracture may lead to early progressive arch collapse, which was
proposed by Anderson et al.5
Diagnosis
Positive Silfverskiöld test: A gastrocnemius contracture is identified if dorsiflexion is less than
10° with the knee extended that improves with the knee flexed.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
First line of treatment for isolated gastrocnemius contracture
Techniques/Procedures
Often successful and consists of diminished intensity of activities, physical therapy with
eccentric strengthening and modalities (eg, iontophoresis, phonophoresis, ultrasonography),
NSAIDs, ice, heel lifts, and night splints
Stretching is the mainstay of nonsurgical management.
Outcomes
Nonsurgical management results in 50% to 98% patient satisfaction at 2 years.6,7
Mean duration of symptoms is approximately 11 months.8
Only 50% of patients had complete resolution of pain (otherwise intermittent or daily pain and
discomfort).8
Surgical Management
Indications
If nonsurgical management fails, gastrocnemius recession may successfully relieve refractory
foot pain with an acceptable complication profile. Indications for gastrocnemius recession
have been expanded to include:
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
9/19

Neuropathic forefoot ulcers
Failed nonsurgical management of the following controversial indications:
Insertional and non-insertional Achilles tendinopathy
Midfoot arthritis
Hallux valgus
Lateral ankle instability
Arch pain without radiographic abnormality
Calcaneal apophysitis
Plantar fasciitis/fibromas
Achilles tendinosis
Early-onset diabetic Charcot arthropathy
Contraindications
High-level athletes should be cautioned with regard to potential partial loss of plantar flexion
strength of the ankle. Theoretically, the triceps surae accounts for approximately 80% to 90%
of plantar flexion strength,9 with the gastrocnemius contributing 40% to 43% of total
strength.10
Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
Several surgical techniques can increase ankle dorsiflexion, correcting an equinus deformity.
These different surgical procedures are determined by the level at which the recession takes
place and what portion of the muscle is being recessed. The more proximal the recession, the
more stable the lengthening but the lesser degree of correction. The more distal the recession,
the less stable the release (ie, a prolonged period of immobilization may be required);
however, a greater degree of dorsiflexion is achieved. (Resource 1).

Preoperative Planning
The original gastrocnemius recession technique was described by Silfverskiöld, in which
a transverse incision is made in the popliteal fossa, and both heads of the gastrocnemius
muscle are released just distal to the knee joint. More distally, the Baumann technique
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
10/19

involves transecting the gastrocnemius muscle aponeurosis proximal to the
myotendinous junction. The Strayer procedure is performed at the level of the
gastrocnemius musculotendinous junction and is an isolated release of the
gastrocnemius tendon.
The most distal procedures are Achilles tendon lengthening techniques, including the
Hoke procedure, which involves three hemi-sections of the Achilles tendon (two medial
and one lateral hemi-section) or Z-lengthening (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Illustrations of the leg show the level of recession or lengthening of the triceps
surae muscle according to the following surgical techniques: Silfverskiöld (A), Baumann
(B), Strayer/Vulpius (C), Baker (D), Hoke (E), Z-lengthening (F). (Reproduced from
Abdulmassih S, Phisitkul P, Femino JE, Amendola A: Triceps surae contracture:
Implications for foot and ankle surgery. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2013;21[7]:398-407.)
Patient Positioning
The patient may be positioned supine or prone. Patient positioning often is dictated
by concomitant procedures.
All bony prominences should be well padded.
The foot should be prepared into the surgical field to allow for preoperative and
postoperative evaluation of the gastrocnemius contracture via the Silfverskiöld test.
Surgical Approaches
Strayer procedure (Video 1)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
11/19

In the supine position, the preference of the author of this lesson is to make a 2- to
3-cm incision along the posteromedial aspect of the distal third of the leg at the level
of the musculotendinous junction of the gastrocnemius, in line with the posterior
border of the medial malleolus.
With the knee extended on the surgical table, the surgical assistant holds the ankle
in dorsiflexion.
A full-thickness incision is made through the dermis, and the branches of the lesser
saphenous vein frequently are visualized and retracted.
Tenotomy scissors are used to open the superficial fascia of the lower leg, in line
with the skin incision.
At this point, tenotomy scissors are used to transect from medial to lateral across
the gastrocnemius tendon at the musculotendinous junction.
After the transection is complete, a noticeable increase of ankle dorsiflexion should
be observed compared with preoperative motion.
Weight bearing as tolerated in a boot with the use of a single crutch is
recommended for 2 weeks postoperatively.
Video 1 Anderson JG: Video. Strayer Procedure. Grand Rapids, MI, 2021.
Baumann procedure (Video 2)
The patient is placed in the supine position.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
12/19

With the knee extended on the surgical table, a 4- to 8-cm longitudinal incision is
made at the level of the midcalf along the medial aspect of the lower leg, in line with
the medial malleolus.
The saphenous nerve and vein are retracted. The superficial fascia of the lower leg is
opened in line with the skin incision.
A plane between the gastrocnemius and soleus muscle is created via blunt dissection
from medial to lateral.
The plantaris tendon is identified and transected. With the knee extended and the
foot dorsiflexed, a scalpel is used to cut the anterior surface of the gastrocnemius
fascia from medial to lateral without disrupting the muscle fibers of the
gastrocnemius muscle.
The intramuscular septum between the medial and lateral heads of the
gastrocnemius muscle is identified and transected. After the transection is completed,
a noticeable increase in ankle dorsiflexion should be observed compared with
preoperative motion.
Weight bearing as tolerated in a boot with the use of a single crutch is recommended
for 2 weeks postoperatively.
Video 2 Anderson JG: Video. Baumann Procedure. Grand Rapids, MI, 2021.
Proximal medial gastrocnemius recession (modified Silfverskiöld procedure; Video 3)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
13/19

The patient is placed in the prone position.
A 2-cm transverse incision is made along the posterior popliteal fossa,
approximately 1 cm distal to the transverse skin crease.
A transverse incision through the superficial fascia is made in line with skin.
Blunt dissection is made from medial to lateral and then to the proximal medial
gastrocnemius head
The fascia of the medial head of the gastrocnemius is identified and transected
under direct visualization of fascia at all times.
The skin is closed with the use of horizontal mattress sutures.
Weight bearing as tolerated in a boot with the use of a single crutch is
recommended for 2 weeks postoperatively.
Video 3 Anderson JG: Video. Proximal Medial Gastrocnemius Recession. Grand Rapids, MI,
2021.
Postoperative Management
Unless concomitant procedures require protected–weight bearing, patients are
instructed to bear weight as tolerated.
Immobilization in a tall walking boot is recommended for 2 weeks postoperatively.
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
14/19

Patient selection is important in determining the appropriate procedure to perform
(Bauman, Strayer, or proximal medial gastrocnemius recession).
The sural nerve should be directly visualized as the gastrocnemius is being sharply
transected to minimize the risk of iatrogenic neuroma and postoperative neuropathy.
Complete gastrocnemius release should include complete release of the
gastrocnemius tendon and the plantaris. Incomplete release may lead to
postoperative completion of the tear, which may be perceived as an audible pop with
subsequent swelling. Postoperative swelling may lead to avoidable evaluation for
deep vein thrombosis at an urgent care facility or emergency department.
Complications
Pain
Maskill et al11 reported substantial improvements in visual analog scale scores from 8.1 to 1.9
in patients with plantar fasciitis, from 7.5 to 2.2 in patients with metatarsalgia, and from 9.3 to
3.3 in patients with arch pain preoperatively and postoperatively, respectively.
Infection
Minimal risk of infection is associated with gastrocnemius recession.
Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
No studies have specifically investigated the risk of deep vein thrombosis/venous
thromboembolism associated with gastrocnemius recession.
Neural Injury/Nerve Palsy
The sural nerve is at risk during gastrocnemius recession; however, no studies have specifically
investigated the risk of sural nerve injury associated with gastrocnemius recession. Several
studies have reported a low incidence (zero cases) of sural neuropathy after gastrocnemius
recession.11,12
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:16 PM
AAOS | Gastrocnemius Contracture
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001012
15/19

Weakness
According to Duthon et al,13strength between the two legs was equal 1 year after
gastrocnemius recession for the management of isolated Achilles tendinopathy.
At 18 months after gastrocnemius recession as part of a more complicated correction,
strength has been reported to be as high as 82% compared with the unaffected side.13
Outcomes
Gastrocnemius recession typically results in 10° to 20° of improved dorsiflexion with
decreased pressure under the medial forefoot14 (Resource 2).
The mean time for return to physical activity was 7.5 months (range, 2 to 24 months)
(Resource 3).
Maskill et al11 reported substantial improvements in visual analog scale scores from 8.1 to 1.9
in patients with plantar fasciitis, from 7.5 to 2.2 in patients with metatarsalgia, and from 9.3 to
3.3 in patients with arch pain preoperatively and postoperatively, respectively.
Diabetic foot ulcer

Outcomes
The advantages of performing gastrocnemius recession or an Achilles tendon
lengthening in patients with diabetes mellitus have been established for some time.
Mueller et al15 followed up with patients with diabetes mellitus and neuropathic ulcers
who underwent treatment via total contact casting or Achilles tendon lengthening. The
authors reported a 75% lower incidence of ulcer recurrence at 7 months and a 52%
lower incidence of ulcer recurrence at 2 years in patients who underwent Achilles tendon
lengthening.
Similarly, gastrocnemius recession via the Vulpius procedure in combination with select
lengthening of peroneal tendons is associated with high success rates, with
Laborde16 reporting healing in 19 of 20 neuropathic ulcers, with only 3 reported
recurrences.
